newsitem.title: USA: Intel Q1 processor price cuts "minimal".
newsitem.headline: Intel Q1 processor price cuts "minimal".

text.p: Intel Corp said it cut pricing for the first quarter on some microprocessor lines, but left pricing unchanged on its higher end Pentium Pro chips, in a move analysts showed strong continued demand for the chips.

Securities nalysts said the price cuts were less than expected and a sign that demand remains strong for Intel microprocessors, which serve as the mechanical "brains" for about 90 percent of the world's personal computers.

In a statement, Intel announced quarterly pricing levels for its Pentium chips, used in lower-end consumer oriented personal computers and Pentium Pro chips, used to build more high-powered corporate and technical machines.

The company said its Pentium Pro 166 is now priced at $627, while 200 megahertz Pentium Pro chips would remain at $525 and $1,035, depending on the amount of memory available. These prices are unchanged from fourth quarter levels.
For its lower-end Pentiums, Intel said its 133 megahertz model was now priced at $134, a decline of about 34 percent from its fourth quarter level.
It said its 100 megahertz Pentium is $106, which would represent no change from the prior quarter, while the 150 megahertz version runs $161, down about 42 percent from the fourth quarter level.
The 200 megahertz Pentium was $498, down two percent from $509 in the fourth quarter, while the recently introduced 200 megahertz Pentium with MMX multimedia technology runs $539, the company said.
All prices quoted are for microprocessors purchased in batches of 1,000 units. Products ordered in larger volumes may receive lower pricing, the company said.

Price setting by the world's dominant supplier of computer chips is a closely watched quarterly ritual that directly affects the pricing for new computers in the following months. It is also taken as an indicator of the health of the market.
Intel has traditionally used regular price reductions on its microprocessor products to spur demand for the increasingly powerful chips.

However, in recent quarters, Intel has been selling every Pentium Pro chip it can produce, postponing the need to cut prices. Of course, foregoing more aggressive price reductions translates directly into higher bottom line profitablity.
In a published note, John Geraghty, who covers Intel for CS First Boston, labeled the latest quarterly pricing changes "minimal."
"The continuing lower rate of price decline, relative to past experience, continues to emphasize that (Intel) is seeing exceptional market demand for its product line," he said.
"This further solidifies our contention that (excellent) demand continues and (Intel's earnings per share) results in 1997 will be sharply higher," Geraghty wrote.

The First Boston analyst reiterated his buy rating on Intel stock and his $200 price target and noted that, "Despite its strong performance in 1996, we still believe INTC will continue to sharply outperform the market in 1997."
Intel shares were up 2-1/4 to 157 in early U.S. third market trading Thursday.
